And he sent troops to subdue the mountains
and to cut off the roads against the Kurds.
And because the season was winter,
and heavy snows lay upon the tops of the mountains where the Kurds were,
the troops of the Mongols were not able to harm them,
nor to gain power over them.
Therefore, they returned to the plain,
where there were poor Kurdish peasants and agricultural laborers who paid tribute;
they took them captive and killed [them],
and plundered and burned their houses and their provisions.
These poor people were especially harmed by certain mountaineers who were with the Mongols,
those who are called Qāyāshāyē (Qāyāchāyē? {OCR?}).
For these were Christians who naturally hate the Muslims;
they wrought great destruction and unspeakable devastation upon the Kurds.
They mercilessly killed the men,
and bound women and sons and daughters without number.
And of their provisions, whatever they were able to carry, they carried off,
and the rest they burned with fire.
Therefore, the Muslims were inflamed with wrath against all the Christians because of these mountaineers,
saying:
"Were it not for these mountaineers,
the Mongols would not have harmed the Kurds at all.
For most of the Mongols have become Muslims in our days,
and they are not inclined to harm Muslims,
unless perhaps they are compelled by their chiefs."
Then the Mongols,
when it became summer,
withdrew and departed from {OCR?} the regions of Mosul and Erbil.
The Kurds, however, came down from the tops of the mountains,
and tens of thousands of tribesmen gathered together
and came to the plain.
The inhabitants of the region fled from before them,
and took refuge in the cities and fortresses.
All [the people of] the region of Erbil went up into the fortress,
and immediately the Kurds besieged the fortress.
However, divine providence quenched their fury,
and they were not successful against the fortress at all.
And every time they pressed {OCR?} to fight against it,
seven or eight souls, more or less, were killed of them.
